title: Jeremiah 2:14–28
context: The LORD continues the same oracle through Jeremiah. The LORD asks whether Israel is a slave, born into slavery, and why the people have become a captive. Young lions have roared and laid the land waste; cities are burned and empty. The children of Memphis and Tahpanhes have broken the crown of the head—Egyptian places whose exact campaign and site should be hedged. The people have brought this on themselves by forsaking the LORD who led them. What do they gain by going to Egypt to drink the waters of the Shihor, or to Assyria to drink the waters of the River? Shihor is often taken as an Egyptian waterway, and the River as the Euphrates; both identifications are commonly offered and are held lightly. Their own wickedness will correct them, and their backsliding will rebuke them; it is an evil and bitter thing that they have forsaken the LORD, and his fear is not in them. Long ago he broke off their yoke, but they said they would not serve, and on every high hill and under every green tree they bowed themselves, unfaithful in the way the book names as playing the prostitute. The LORD had planted a noble vine, a pure and faithful seed, and they have become a foreign vine; washing with lye cannot take the iniquity away. They claim they are not defiled and have not gone after the Baals; the LORD points to the valley and to a restless going after others. In trouble they will cry to be saved, but they have as many gods as towns, and those gods cannot save. The marriage and craving images in 2:20–25 are to be handled soberly and without graphic detail: they name idolatry as unfaithfulness and as determined pursuit, not a scene to be retold in physical terms.

verses.text: Is Israel a slave? Is he born into slavery? Why has he become a captive?
verses.arminianNotes:
“Is Israel a slave? Is he born into slavery? Why has he become a captive?” The questions expect the answer that Israel was not naturally a slave, and yet has become a captive. The shame is that a people belonging to the LORD now stand as if in bondage.

Arminian readers hear a real lament and a real question about responsibility: if Israel was not born a slave, the captivity is a condition they have come into, which the next verses will tie to forsaking the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same questions as the LORD’s: Israel is not by birth a slave, so the captivity is a grievous reversal, to be explained by the forsaking that follows, not by some original slave status.

Shared ground: the questions are rhetorical, and they prepare the charge. There is no party contrast over Israel’s status as the LORD’s people.

verses.text: The young lions have roared at him and raised their voices. They have made his land waste. His cities are burned up, without inhabitant.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The young lions have roared at him and raised their voices. They have made his land waste.” The cities are “burned up, without inhabitant.” The lions are foes who have ravaged the land. The verse does not name them; later readers sometimes think of one empire or another, and that identification is held lightly here.

Arminian readers take the wasted land and burned cities as a real disaster already in view or underway, a fruit of the people’s leaving, not a mere figure without historical weight.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear a land laid waste and cities burned, the work of roaring lions as the verse’s picture of invading power. The LORD is describing what has happened to the land, and the identification of the lions can wait for clearer lines.

Both traditions keep the image and the ruin together. The verse does not require a named enemy.

verses.text: The children also of Memphis and Tahpanhes have broken the crown of your head.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The children also of Memphis and Tahpanhes have broken the crown of your head.” Memphis and Tahpanhes are Egyptian places—Memphis a well-known city of Lower Egypt, Tahpanhes often associated with the eastern Delta—but the exact sites and the exact blow intended here should be hedged. “broken the crown of your head” is language of humiliation or injury, not a cue to reconstruct a single battle.

Arminian readers take the line as a charge that Egypt has already shamed the people, a fruit of the foreign trusts the next verses will name, not an incidental travel notice.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also read a humiliation at the hands of Memphis and Tahpanhes. The crown of the head is broken, and the names point toward Egypt, without the verse itself narrating a full campaign.

Shared ground: Egypt is in view, and the damage is real. Precise identifications remain modest.

verses.text: “Haven’t you brought this on yourself, in that you have forsaken the LORD your God, when he led you by the way?
verses.arminianNotes:
“Haven’t you brought this on yourself, in that you have forsaken the LORD your God, when he led you by the way?” The disaster is not unexplained, and it is not blamed on the LORD’s leading. They have brought it on themselves by forsaking the God who led them.

Arminian readers take the question as a real assignment of responsibility. The people forsook the LORD while he was leading them, and the harm is their own doing in that sense.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same “Haven’t you brought this on yourself” as the LORD’s verdict. The forsaking, not a failure in his leading, is the reason named.

Both traditions accept the charge. The verse is shared ground on guilt, not a contrast over how leading and leaving relate in a philosophical scheme.

verses.text: Now what do you gain by going to Egypt, to drink the waters of the Shihor? Or why do you go on the way to Assyria, to drink the waters of the River?
verses.arminianNotes:
“Now what do you gain by going to Egypt, to drink the waters of the Shihor? Or why do you go on the way to Assyria, to drink the waters of the River?” The people are pictured as going south and north for water, for help or alliance. Shihor is often taken as an Egyptian waterway; the River is often taken as the Euphrates. Both readings are common and should be left hedged. The contrast with the spring of living waters in 2:13 may be felt, without forcing every water image in the chapter into one tight scheme.

Arminian readers hear a real question about profit: what is gained by these journeys? The trusts in Egypt and Assyria are chosen, and they will not satisfy.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same questions as the LORD’s exposure of failed policy and failed trust. Drinking from Shihor or from the River is set against the God they have forsaken, and it will not profit them.

Shared ground: Egypt and Assyria are the wrong waters. The identifications of Shihor and the River may be offered modestly.

verses.text: “Your own wickedness will correct you, and your backsliding will rebuke you. Know therefore and see that it is an evil and bitter thing, that you have forsaken the LORD your God, and that my fear is not in you,” says the Lord, GOD of Armies.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Your own wickedness will correct you, and your backsliding will rebuke you.” It is “an evil and bitter thing, that you have forsaken the LORD your God,” and “my fear is not in you” The correction and the rebuke rise from their own wickedness and backsliding. Forsaking the LORD is named as evil and bitter, and the lack of fear of him is part of the charge.

Arminian readers take “Your own wickedness will correct you” as a real moral consequence: the path they have chosen will itself turn on them, a rebuke they could have avoided by not forsaking him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear wickedness and backsliding as the instruments of correction. The LORD names the forsaking as evil and bitter, and the absence of his fear as the inner side of that leaving.

Both traditions share the verdict. The verse does not require a fork over whether the correction is natural consequence or the LORD’s appointed rebuke; both can be heard in the line.

verses.text: “For long ago I broke off your yoke, and burst your bonds. You said, ‘I will not serve;’ for on every high hill and under every green tree you bowed yourself, playing the prostitute.
verses.arminianNotes:
“For long ago I broke off your yoke, and burst your bonds.” They said, “I will not serve;” and “on every high hill and under every green tree you bowed yourself, playing the prostitute.” The LORD recalls a liberation, then a refusal to serve, then worship on the hills and under the trees. The last phrase is the book’s language for unfaithfulness to him, usually of idolatry at the high places. It should be left in that sober sense, without graphic expansion.

Arminian readers hear a real refusal after a real breaking of the yoke. “I will not serve” is their word, and the bowing on the hills is a chosen unfaithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the broken yoke as the LORD’s past act, and the “I will not serve” as the people’s reply, followed by the hill-and-tree worship the verse names. The unfaithfulness is theirs, and the language is kept restrained.

Shared ground: liberation, refusal, and rival worship belong together here. The imagery is to be explained as unfaithfulness, not retold in physical detail.

verses.text: Yet I had planted you a noble vine, a pure and faithful seed. How then have you turned into the degenerate branches of a foreign vine to me?
verses.arminianNotes:
“Yet I had planted you a noble vine, a pure and faithful seed. How then have you turned into the degenerate branches of a foreign vine to me?” The LORD had planted what was noble and faithful; the people have become like a foreign vine. The question “How then” underlines the strangeness of the change, not a botany lesson.

Arminian readers hear a real degeneration from a real planting. The vine was planted pure and faithful, and the turning into foreign branches is the people’s own departure from that planting.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also start from the LORD’s planting of a noble vine, a pure and faithful seed, and from the grief of the change into degenerate, foreign branches. The contrast is between what he planted and what they have become.

Both traditions share the image. It is of a piece with the forsaking already named, not a separate party argument about seed and perseverance.

verses.text: For though you wash yourself with lye, and use much soap, yet your iniquity is marked before me,” says the Lord GOD.
verses.arminianNotes:
“For though you wash yourself with lye, and use much soap, yet your iniquity is marked before me,” says the Lord GOD. Outward washing, however strong, does not remove the mark of iniquity the LORD sees. The stain is not a matter of dirt that soap can lift.

Arminian readers take the line as a warning against treating guilt as something they can scrub off. The iniquity remains marked before God until it is dealt with as iniquity, not as a surface problem.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same impossibility: lye and soap cannot unmark what is marked before the Lord GOD. The iniquity is known to him, and ceremonial or outward cleansing does not erase it.

Shared ground: washing cannot hide the guilt. The verse is not a contrast over the means of forgiveness, which this line does not yet name.

verses.text: “How can you say, ‘I am not defiled. I have not gone after the Baals’? See your way in the valley. Know what you have done. You are a swift dromedary traversing her ways,
verses.arminianNotes:
“How can you say, ‘I am not defiled. I have not gone after the Baals’? See your way in the valley. Know what you have done.” They claim purity and deny the Baals; the LORD tells them to look at their way in the valley and to know what they have done. Which valley is meant is not certain here and should be hedged. The swift dromedary traversing her ways is a picture of restless running; it should be kept brief and not made graphic, especially as the next verse continues the image.

Arminian readers hear a false claim of innocence, contradicted by a way that can be seen. The denial is their own word, and it does not stand.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the quoted claim as the people’s self-defense, which the LORD overturns by pointing to the valley and to what they have done. The running animal image underlines how they go, without needing to be pressed for extra detail.

Shared ground: the claim “I am not defiled” is false. The valley and the dromedary are the LORD’s evidence, modestly described.

verses.text: a wild donkey used to the wilderness, that sniffs the wind in her craving. When she is in heat, who can turn her away? All those who seek her will not weary themselves. In her month, they will find her.
verses.arminianNotes:
The picture continues with “a wild donkey used to the wilderness, that sniffs the wind in her craving.” “When she is in heat, who can turn her away?” The verse uses a strong animal image for unrestrained pursuit. It should be handled in one sober point: the people, in the LORD’s charge, go after what they crave and will not be turned aside. There is no need to linger on the language, and no party contrast in the image itself.

Arminian readers take the unrestrained going as the people’s determined will, a craving they will not give up, which the next verse will put into their own mouth as a refusal to stop.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also read a picture of determined pursuit that will not be turned away. The LORD is describing how set the people are on their path, and the notes should not turn the verse into a study of the image beyond that charge.

Both traditions keep the line brief and sober. The meaning is unfaithful, unrestrained going after others, not a cue for graphic comment.

verses.text: “Keep your feet from being bare, and your throat from thirst. But you said, ‘It is in vain. No, for I have loved strangers, and I will go after them.’
verses.arminianNotes:
“Keep your feet from being bare, and your throat from thirst.” But they said, “It is in vain. No, for I have loved strangers, and I will go after them.” A warning to stop is answered with “It is in vain” and with a resolve to go after strangers. The love of strangers here is the choice of other gods and other helps, to be read in that sober sense.

Arminian readers hear a real offer to stop, refused in so many words. They say the warning is vain, and they will go after those they have loved; the refusal is theirs.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the quoted reply as the people’s settled word: they will go after strangers, and they call the warning vain. The LORD records their resolve, and it stands as evidence in the case he is making.

Shared ground: they refuse to stop. The “strangers” are the rival trusts already in view, not a prompt for graphic retelling.

verses.text: As the thief is ashamed when he is found, so the house of Israel is ashamed— they, their kings, their princes, their priests, and their prophets,
verses.arminianNotes:
“As the thief is ashamed when he is found, so the house of Israel is ashamed— they, their kings, their princes, their priests, and their prophets,” Shame comes when the thief is found. The house of Israel, from kings to prophets, is put in that position. The shame is public, and it reaches every rank already named in the book’s earlier charges.

Arminian readers take the comparison as a real exposure. The house is ashamed as a thief is ashamed when caught, a shame that belongs to their being found out, not a shame they can deny.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear a shame like the thief’s when found, covering kings, princes, priests, and prophets with the people. The whole house is in view, and the shame is the LORD’s verdict on what will come to light.

Both traditions share the comparison. There is no party contrast over which office is included; the verse lists them.

verses.text: who tell wood, ‘You are my father,’ and a stone, ‘You have given birth to me,’ for they have turned their back to me, and not their face, but in the time of their trouble they will say, ‘Arise, and save us!’
verses.arminianNotes:
They “tell wood, ‘You are my father,’ and a stone, ‘You have given birth to me,’” and “they have turned their back to me, and not their face,” but in trouble they will say, “Arise, and save us!” Wood and stone are treated as father and as the one who gave them birth. They turn the back, not the face, to the LORD, and then cry for rescue when trouble comes.

Arminian readers hear a real inconsistency: they assign to idols what belongs to God, turn away, and still call on him in trouble, a pattern they can and should abandon.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the quoted address to wood and stone as the depth of the idolatry, and the later cry “Arise, and save us!” as a prayer that does not undo the turned back. The LORD is recording how they will speak when trouble comes.

Shared ground: idolatry and a fair-weather cry stand together. The verse is a charge, not a fork over whether such a cry can ever be heard.

verses.text: “But where are your gods that you have made for yourselves? Let them arise, if they can save you in the time of your trouble, for you have as many gods as you have towns, O Judah.
verses.arminianNotes:
“But where are your gods that you have made for yourselves? Let them arise, if they can save you in the time of your trouble, for you have as many gods as you have towns, O Judah.” The cry of the last verse is met with a question. The gods they made are to arise, if they can save; Judah has as many gods as towns. The challenge is the helplessness of what they have made.

Arminian readers take the question as a real test of those gods. They cannot save, and the people are being pressed to see that the trusts they chose will fail in trouble.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same challenge as the LORD’s exposure of handmade gods. They are many, town by town, and they cannot arise to save in the time of trouble.

Both traditions share the point. The verse is not a debate about the number of shrines so much as a charge that Judah’s many gods cannot save.
